assumptions: assume 1 engineer + 1 designer, 6 weeks, and real spend money for the generation ladder (their full film priced ~$238)
you can start smaller: one shot class, one priced gate, one table of verdicts — the calibration view is what takes the weeks
the character-reference locking is the part that needs image-model skill, not plumbing
value.why: the agent choreography is a weekend; the honest parts are the ledger, the calibration views, and the locked-identity image pipeline

data_and_models.value: Model choice is per task shape across the Gemini family on Vertex AI (Pro for whole-script reasoning, Flash for rule-bound generation, Flash-Lite for batch); data is the team's own generation ledger in ClickHouse (shot class, parameters, tier, attempt number, keep/again, cost, duration, model) feeding two materialised views for pass rates and prediction calibration; Firestore holds state, Cloud Storage holds media.

how_it_works.value: One Cloud Run service shipping frontend and backend together; Gemini family on Vertex AI; Firestore for state; Cloud Storage for media; ClickHouse for the learning loop reached through the official mcp-clickhouse server. Model assignment is a cost decision by shape of work: Pro holds the whole screenplay in mind at once (37 scenes to chapters, resolving that 'Luna' and '月音' are the same character), Flash does rule-bound work (prompt writing, subtitle translation, counting people in a finished clip), Flash-Lite does high-volume low-judgement batches. Screenplay parsing keeps the expensive model because it is the foundation: the premium is ~$0.11 on a 90-page script and an error there propagates invisibly. Money gates are schema state transitions, never prompt instructions, because a probabilistic component cannot guarantee a hard requirement.

how_they_tested.value: No test suite is published; the evidence offered is an A/B measurement (29%→49% on the same shots), a seeded deliberate ×0.92 bias in the ledger to prove the calibration view catches optimism, and stated per-shot outcome logging.

limits_they_disclosed.value: $150 of credits against $1 per ten seconds of footage meant no 'just generate it again'; the full film prices near $238 and is still unshot. In production debugging: a 200 response with a 30 MB file and no burned-in subtitles, because the container had no fonts and ffmpeg exits 0 regardless; a 300 s video timeout that never fired because requests measures the gap between reads, so the platform killed it at 900 s and the failure record was lost with it; a health endpoint that reported '12 fonts, 4 CJK' while fontconfig's config file was missing, i.e. a check that looked like verification and was not; two copies of the same learning-loop component drifting, one reading the wrong key and quietly showing 0 for three days. Adopted rules: degrading is fine, degrading silently is not; demo build and production build are one image, one commit, differing only by an env var.

what_breaks_first.value: The success-rate estimate. Below a few hundred logged shots per shot class the displayed percentage is a prior wearing a lab coat, so build the calibration view (predicted vs observed) in week one or you are shipping confidence theatre. Second to break: prompt-injection-free subtitle burn-in on a fresh container, which is exactly the bug they documented (ffmpeg exits 0 with no fonts).

what_it_does.value: User drops a screenplay. The system reads it whole, splits it into chapters, breaks chapters into shots, casts characters, writes prompts, generates footage, then inspects what it made: if shot 3 contains a person who should not be there it notices and folds that into the retry instruction. The user presses keep or again. Before any spend it quotes odds: this chapter is 12 shots, ~$4.50, about half will pass first try. Casting is a hard gate; a character reference costs $0.02 while a shot costs $1 and a finished segment ~$20, so every decision is pushed down the cost ladder. Face is an input, look is an output: an uploaded photo is locked as identity while only the style re-renders, and wardrobe is per chapter. Style buttons carry their own success adjustment (photorealistic −10pt vs animation +12/+15pt). Every generation and every keep/again verdict is written to ClickHouse, so once enough similar shots exist the estimate switches from built-in priors to that user's own numbers and says which one you are looking at plus the sample size. After casting, every prompt is exportable.

what_it_is.value: Drop a screenplay; nine agents read it, cast it, price it, shoot it, and watch what they made — with the quote shown before you press the button.

what_to_steal.value: Two moves, and they compose: (1) quote the cost and the pass rate before the button, and push every hesitation down the price ladder (settle a character at $0.02, not $1); (2) log every verdict row into a store you can query, then let the estimate switch from your priors to the user's own measured numbers and label which one they are reading, with sample size. Also steal 'the money gate is a schema transition, not a prompt'.

what_it_does.value: She drags the file on; ninety seconds later she sees 37 scenes, 6 characters, and the sentence 'this chapter is 12 shots, it'll cost $4.50, about half will come out right first time'. When a line trips the content filter they generate the shot anyway and move the line into the subtitle layer, so no word of her script changes. Every prompt exports as text, markdown or JSON.

Next.js 15 on Vercel, Supabase for Google sign-in, Cloudflare R2 for storage, Upstash for rate limiting, Stripe for live payments, PostHog for analytics.

how_they_tested.value: No unit or eval suite is described; the measurable loop they do have is product analytics - PostHog funnel inspection that found conversion bugs and mispriced ad targeting. That is a real feedback mechanism, just not a quality gate on output fidelity.

limits_they_disclosed.value: A free-render tool attracts abuse, so sign-in is mandatory and generation is hard-capped; Google blocks sign-in inside Facebook and Instagram in-app browsers, so they built an escape that routes those users to a real browser; the model in the original plan was retired mid-build and the pipeline was migrated with no downtime.

also sells speed-to-artifact to solo sellers; this one owns the production concern the others skip

what_breaks_first.value: Taste. 'Print-ready' is a per-style judgement, and a paid print-on-demand seller returns goods that merely look like a filter - there is no fidelity metric anywhere in the capture, no style-level acceptance rate, and no human review loop. The single-provider dependency is the other one: they already survived one model retirement mid-build, and the pipeline still has one throat to choke.

what_it_does.value: Upload a photo, pick one of ten styles (pencil, charcoal, ink, watercolor, line art and others), get a high-resolution sketch exportable for print up to 4K. Three free renders after one-tap Google sign-in, then credits. Running in production.

what_it_is.value: Photo to print-ready sketch in ten styles at up to 4K, live in production, with a free tier that is defensible because sign-in, caps and rate limits were engineered first.

what_to_steal.value: Engineer the free tier as the abuse surface first: sign-in as the price of a render, a hard generation cap, and an explicit rate limiter as its own component. Then use the cheap model to read and the expensive model to render, so the cost curve, not the vendor's price list, decides how much you can give away.

name: SketchWish
verdict_reasons: soundness 0.68 over 64% of the rubric; 0 named unknown(s) remain → publishable with caveats
worth_note: Not a photo filter but a small company assembled correctly: a cheap vision pass protecting fidelity, an image model doing the rendering, third-party auth, storage, quota and payments so the free tier stays solvent, plus two genuinely hard-won findings - that model deprecation mid-build is an operational risk to design for, and that in-app browsers break Google sign-in so the funnel needs an escape hatch. Most hackathon 'live product' claims are demos; this one names its own margin.
